{{Statistical mechanics}}

The '''virial expansion''' is a model of thermodynamic [[equations of state]]. It expresses the [[pressure]] {{Mvar|P}} of a gas in local [[Thermodynamic equilibrium|equilibrium]] as a [[power series]] of the [[density]]. This equation may be represented in terms of the [[compressibility factor]], {{mvar|Z}}, as
<math display="block">Z \equiv \frac{P}{RT\rho} = A + B\rho + C\rho^2 + \cdots</math>
This equation was first proposed by [[Heike Kamerlingh Onnes|Kamerlingh Onnes]].<ref name="onnes">Kamerlingh Onnes, H., [https://dwc.knaw.nl/DL/publications/PU00014258.pdf "Expression of the equation of state of gases and liquids by means of series"], ''KNAW, Proceedings'', 4, 1901-1902, Amsterdam, 125-147 (1902).</ref> The terms {{Mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}} represent the [[virial coefficients]]. The leading coefficient {{mvar|A}} is defined as the constant value of 1, which ensures that the equation reduces to the [[ideal gas]] expression as the gas density approaches zero.

== Second and third virial coefficients ==
The second, {{mvar|B}}, and third, {{mvar|C}}, virial coefficients have been studied extensively and tabulated for many fluids for more than a century. Two of the most extensive compilations are in the books by Dymond<ref>Dymond J. D., Wilhoit R. C., Virial coefficients of pure gases and mixtures, Springer (2003).</ref><ref>Dymond J. H., Smith E. B., Virial coefficients of pure gases and mixtures. A critical compilation, Oxford University Press, 1st Edition (1969), 2nd Edition (1980).</ref> and the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]]'s Thermo Data Engine Database<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://trc.nist.gov/tde.html|title = ThermoData Engine}}</ref> and its Web Thermo Tables.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wtt-lite.nist.gov/wtt-lite/|title = NIST/TRC Web Thermo Tables (WTT): Critically Evaluated Thermophysical Property Data}}</ref> Tables of second and third virial coefficients of many fluids are included in these compilations.

[[File:Argon b c.jpg|thumb|The 2nd and 3rd virial coefficients of argon]]

== Casting equations of the state into virial form ==

Most equations of state can be reformulated and cast in virial equations to evaluate and compare their implicit second and third virial coefficients. The seminal [[van der Waals equation]] of state<ref>van der Waals J. D., On the continuity of the gaseous and liquid states (Doctoral dissertation). Universiteit Leiden (1873).</ref> was proposed in 1873:
<math display="block">P = \frac{RT}{\left(v-b\right)} - \frac{a}{v^2}</math>
where {{math|1=''v'' = 1/''ρ''}} is [[molar volume]]. It can be rearranged by expanding {{math|1/(''v'' − ''b'')}} into a [[Taylor series]]:
<math display="block">Z = 1 + \left(b-\frac{a}{RT}\right)\rho + b^2\rho^2 + b^3\rho^3 + \cdots</math>

In the van der Waals equation, the second virial coefficient has roughly the correct behavior, as it decreases monotonically when the temperature is lowered. The third and higher virial coefficients are independent of temperature and are not correct, especially at low temperatures. 

Almost all subsequent equations of state are derived from the van der Waals equation, like those from Dieterici,<ref>Dieterici(7), C. Dieterici, Ann. Phys. Chem. Wiedemanns Ann. 69, 685 (1899).</ref> Berthelot,<ref>D. Berthelot, D., in Travaux et Mémoires du Bureau international des Poids et Mesures – Tome XIII (Paris: Gauthier-Villars, 1907).</ref> Redlich-Kwong,<ref>Redlich, Otto; Kwong, J. N. S. On The Thermodynamics of Solutions, Chem. Rev. 44 (1): 233–244 (1949).</ref> and Peng-Robinson<ref>Peng, D. Y.; Robinson, D. B., A New Two-Constant Equation of State. Industrial and Engineering Chemistry: Fundamentals. 15: 59–64 (1976).</ref> suffer from the singularity introduced by {{math|1/(v - b)}}.

Other equations of state, started by Beattie and Bridgeman,<ref>Beattie, J. A., and Bridgeman, O. C., A new equation of state for fluids, Proc. Am. Acad. Art Sci., 63, 229-308 (1928).</ref> are more closely related to virial equations, and show to be more accurate in representing behavior of fluids in both gaseous and liquid phases.{{Citation needed|date=September 2021}} The Beattie-Bridgeman equation of state, proposed in 1928, 
<math display="block">p=\frac{RT}{v^2}\left(1-\frac{c}{vT^3}\right)(v+B)-\frac{A}{v^2}</math>
where
*<math>A = A_0 \left(1 - \frac{a}{v} \right)</math>
*<math>B = B_0 \left(1 - \frac{b}{v} \right)</math>
can be rearranged as
<math display="block">Z=1 + \left(B_0 -\frac{A_0}{RT} - \frac{c}{T^3}\right) \rho - \left(B_0 b-\frac{A_0 a}{RT} + \frac{B_0 c}{T^3}\right) \rho^2 + \left(\frac{B_0 b c}{T^3}\right) \rho^3 </math>The Benedict-Webb-Rubin equation of state<ref>Benedict, Manson; Webb, George B.; Rubin, Louis C., An Empirical Equation for Thermodynamic Properties of Light Hydrocarbons and Their Mixtures: I. Methane, Ethane, Propane, and n-Butane, Journal of Chemical Physics, 8 (4): 334–345 (1940).</ref> of 1940 represents better isotherms below the critical temperature:
<math display="block">Z = 1 + \left(B_0 -\frac{A_0}{RT} - \frac{C_0}{RT^3}\right) \rho + \left(b-\frac{a}{RT}\right) \rho^2 + \left(\frac{\alpha a}{RT}\right) \rho^5 + \frac{c\rho^2}{RT^3}\left(1 + \gamma\rho^2\right)\exp\left(-\gamma\rho^2\right)</math>

More improvements were achieved by Starling<ref name="starling">Starling, Kenneth E., Fluid Properties for Light Petroleum Systems, Gulf Publishing Company, p. 270 (1973).</ref> in 1972:
<math display="block">Z = 1 + \left(B_0 -\frac{A_0}{RT} - \frac{C_0}{RT^3} + \frac{D_0}{RT^4} - \frac{E_0}{RT^5}\right) \rho + \left(b-\frac{a}{RT}-\frac{d}{RT^2}\right) \rho^2 + \alpha\left(\frac{a}{RT}+\frac{d}{RT^2}\right) \rho^5 + \frac{c\rho^2}{RT^3}\left(1 + \gamma\rho^2\right)\exp\left(-\gamma\rho^2\right)</math>

The following are plots of reduced second and third virial coefficients against reduced temperature according to Starling:<ref name="starling" />

[[File: BWRS-reduced 1.jpg|thumb|The 2nd and 3rd virial coefficients for 12 fluids]]

The exponential terms in the last two equations correct the third virial coefficient so that the isotherms in the liquid phase can be represented correctly. The exponential term converges rapidly as ρ increases, and if only the first two terms in its Taylor expansion series are taken, <math>1-\gamma\rho^2</math>, and multiplied with <math>1 + \gamma\rho^2</math>, the result is <math>1 - \gamma^2\rho^4</math>, which contributes a <math>c / RT^3</math> term to the third virial coefficient, and one term to the eighth virial coefficient, which can be ignored.{{Original research inline|date=May 2024}}

After the expansion of the exponential terms, the Benedict-Webb-Rubin and Starling equations of state have this form:
<math display="block">Z = 1 + b\rho_r + c\rho_r^2 + f\rho_r^5</math><!-- (This portion is a set of opinions, with a non-neutral tone, and with no citations.  Therefore, it is hidden.  However, if properly written, it could provide useful hints to the proper use of virial EOSs.)
The original study of Kamerlingh Onnes <ref name="onnes" /> omitted the fourth virial coefficient ''D'', and designated the higher terms as a residue in the virial equation. Unfortunately, the significance of the first three third virial terms has never been fully appreciated, and their effects on gaseous-liquid equilibrium were masked by other higher virial coefficients in the blind search for precision, with "multi-variable optimization" algorithms or the likes.
It is now clear why Benedict-Webb-Rubin improved on Beattie-Bridgeman's equation of state by adding the complicated exponential term. They ought to have recognized that the third virial coefficient in the gaseous phase was small, but had to be large in the liquid phase. Instead of enlarging the third virial coefficient, they chose to add the strange-looking exponential term, whose sole purpose was to make the third virial coefficient larger at lower temperatures. The Taylor expansion of this exponential term reveals their true intentions.
-->

== Cubic virial equation of state ==
The three-term virial equation or a cubic virial equation of state
<math display="block">Z = 1+B\rho+C\rho^2</math>
has the simplicity of the Van der Waals equation of state without its singularity at {{math|1=''v'' = ''b''}}. Theoretically, the second virial coefficient represents bimolecular attraction forces, and the third virial term represents the repulsive forces among three molecules in close contact.{{Citation needed|date=September 2021}}

With this cubic virial equation, the coefficients B and C can be solved in closed form. Imposing the critical conditions:
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}v}=0  \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}^2P}{\mathrm{d}v^2}=0</math>
The cubic virial equation can be solved to yield:
<math display="block">B = -v_c ,</math> <math display="block"> C = \frac{v_c^2}{3},</math> and <math display="block">Z_c = \frac{P_c v_c}{RT_c} = \frac 1 3.</math>
<math>Z_c</math> is therefore 0.333, compared to 0.375 from the Van der Waals equation.

Between the critical point and the [[triple point]] is the saturation region of fluids. In this region, the gaseous phase coexists with the liquid phase under saturation pressure <math>P_\text{sat}</math>, and the saturation temperature <math>T_\text{sat}</math>. Under the saturation pressure, the liquid phase has a molar volume of <math>v_\text{l}</math>, and the gaseous phase has a molar volume of <math>v_\text{g}</math>. The corresponding molar densities are <math>\rho_\text{l}</math> and <math>\rho_\text{g}</math>. These are the saturation properties needed to compute second and third virial coefficients.

A valid equation of state must produce an isotherm which crosses the horizontal line of <math>P_\text{sat}</math> at <math>v_\text{l}</math> and <math>v_\text{g}</math>, on <math>T_\text{sat}</math>.{{Citation needed|date=September 2021}} Under <math>P_\text{sat}</math> and <math>T_\text{sat}</math>, gas is in equilibrium with liquid. This means that the PρT isotherm has three roots at <math>P_\text{sat}</math>. The cubic virial equation of state at <math>T_\text{sat}</math> is: 
<math display="block">P_\text{sat} = RT_\text{sat} \left(1 + B\rho + C\rho^2\right) \rho</math>
It can be rearranged as:
<math display="block">1 - \frac{RT_\text{sat}}{P_\text{sat}} \left(1 + B\rho + C\rho^2\right) \rho = 0</math>
The factor <math>RT_\text{sat}/P_\text{sat}</math> is the volume of saturated gas according to the [[ideal gas law]], and can be given a unique name <math>v^\text{id}</math>:
<math display="block">v^\text{id} = \frac{RT_\text{sat}}{P_\text{sat}}</math>
In the saturation region, the cubic equation has three roots, and can be written alternatively as:
<math display="block">\left(1 - v_\text{l} \rho \right) \left(1 - v_\text{m} \rho \right) \left(1 - v_\text{g} \rho \right) = 0</math>
which can be expanded as:
<math display="block">1 - \left(v_\text{l} + v_\text{g} + v_m\right)\rho + \left(v_\text{l} v_\text{g} + v_\text{g} v_\text{m} + v_\text{m} v_\text{l}\right)\rho^2 - v_\text{l} v_\text{g} v_\text{m} \rho^3 = 0 </math>
<math>v_\text{m}</math> is a volume of an unstable state between <math>v_\text{l}</math> and <math>v_\text{g}</math>. The cubic equations are identical. Therefore, from the linear terms in these equations, <math>v_m</math> can be solved:
<math display="block">v_\text{m} = v^\text{id} - v_\text{l} - v_\text{g} </math>
From the quadratic terms, ''B'' can be solved:
<math display="block">B = -\frac{\left(v_\text{l} v_\text{g} + v_\text{g} v_\text{m} + v_\text{m} v_\text{l}\right)}{v^\text{id}} </math>
And from the cubic terms, ''C'' can be solved:
<math display="block">C = \frac{v_\text{l} v_\text{g} v_\text{m}}{v^\text{id}} </math>
Since <math>v_\text{l}</math>, <math>v_\text{g}</math> and <math>P_\text{sat}</math> have been tabulated for many fluids with <math>T_\text{sat}</math> as a parameter, ''B'' and ''C'' can be computed in the saturation region of these fluids. The results are generally in agreement with those computed from Benedict-Webb-Rubin and Starling equations of state.{{Citation needed|date=September 2021}}
